content: Psychosis is a mental health condition characterized by the presence of hallucinations and delusions, which can lead to significant distress or noticeable changes in behavior, such as social withdrawal or a flat or blunted emotional state. A first episode of psychosis (FEP) refers to the initial occurrence of these symptoms, which can happen at any age but is most commonly observed in late adolescence or early adulthood. This review focuses on FEP and the early stages of psychosis, collectively referred to as recent-onset psychosis. Specialized early intervention (SEI) teams are community-based mental health teams designed to provide targeted care for individuals experiencing recent-onset psychosis. These teams offer a comprehensive range of treatments, including pharmacological interventions, psychotherapy, psychoeducation, and support for education and employment. They also maintain assertive contact with patients and manage small caseloads to ensure personalized care. SEI treatment is typically time-limited, lasting two to three years, after which patients are either transitioned to primary care or referred to standard adult community mental health teams. However, evidence suggests that the benefits of SEI may not always persist after treatment ends, raising questions about the optimal duration of SEI to achieve sustained long-term outcomes. Extending SEI treatment beyond the standard duration, often up to five years, has been proposed as a strategy to maintain the initial positive outcomes of SEI and potentially improve the long-term course of the illness. This review aimed to compare the effectiveness of extended SEI with treatment as usual (TAU) and with standard SEI followed by TAU (standard SEI + TAU) for individuals with recent-onset psychosis. The review included three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving a total of 780 participants aged 16 to 35 years, all of whom met diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia spectrum disorders or affective psychoses. None of the trials compared extended SEI with TAU directly. Instead, all three studies randomized participants who had already received approximately two years of standard SEI to either extended SEI or standard SEI + TAU. The certainty of evidence for the outcomes assessed ranged from low to very low. The primary outcomes of interest were recovery and disengagement from mental health services. None of the trials reported on recovery, so remission was used as a proxy measure. Three trials reported on remission, with results suggesting a 13% increase in remission rates favoring extended SEI. However, the confidence intervals were wide, indicating a high degree of uncertainty (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.31; 3 trials, 780 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Two trials provided data on disengagement from mental health services. Extended SEI appeared to reduce the rate of disengagement from services (15%) compared to standard SEI + TAU (34%) (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.75; 2 trials, 380 participants; low-certainty evidence). There was no clear evidence of a difference in psychiatric hospital admission rates (RR 1.55, 95% CI 0.68 to 3.52; 1 trial, 160 participants; low-certainty evidence) or the number of days spent in a psychiatric hospital (MD -2.70, 95% CI -8.30 to 2.90; 1 trial, 400 participants; low-certainty evidence). One trial reported on global psychotic symptoms, with results suggesting uncertain evidence of lower symptom severity in the extended SEI group compared to the standard SEI + TAU group (MD -1.90, 95% CI -3.28 to -0.52; 1 trial, 156 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The evidence regarding all-cause mortality was also uncertain, as very few deaths were recorded across the trials (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.64; 3 trials, 780 participants; low-certainty evidence). Similarly, there was very uncertain evidence regarding the impact of extended SEI on global functioning (SMD 0.23, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.76; 2 trials, 560 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The risk of bias was assessed for all three trials. There was a low risk of bias for random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and other biases. However, all three trials had a high risk of bias for blinding of participants and personnel due to the nature of the intervention. Additionally, at least one trial had a high or unclear risk of bias for blinding of outcome assessments and incomplete outcome data. In conclusion, there is preliminary evidence suggesting that extending SEI care may reduce disengagement from mental health services for individuals with recent-onset psychosis. However, evidence for other outcomes, such as remission, global functioning, and symptom severity, remains uncertain due to the low or very low certainty of the available data. Further research with adequately powered studies and consistent outcome measures is needed to draw more definitive conclusions. However, with only one additional ongoing trial identified, it is unlikely that a clear determination of the effectiveness of extended SEI will be available in the near future.
